name: Blue Team — Defense & Detection
tagline: Tools defenders run to detect, hunt, and respond on their own estate: SIEM, endpoint and network telemetry, detection engineering, response automation, and hostile edge hardening.

tools.name: Elastic Stack (ELK)
tools.desc: Reference open-core free SIEM: ships logs via Elastic Agent/Beats into Elasticsearch, renders detections and dashboards in Kibana, and runs the detection engine on EQL/ES|QL, Sigma, and YARA rule content.
tools.when: Your first-stop free SOC when you want one cluster for full-text log search plus security detections and can absorb Elasticsearch operations.
tools.install: docker run -d -p 9200:9200 -e discovery.type=single-node docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:9.5.1 (then add Kibana + Elastic Agent via the docs)

tools.name: Wazuh
tools.desc: Open-source XDR/SIEM pairing an Elastic/OpenSearch backend with a unified agent delivering file-integrity monitoring, security configuration assessment, vulnerability detection, active response, and compliance dashboards.
tools.when: When you want SIEM plus an endpoint agent in one cohesive open bundle with built-in compliance reporting (PCI-DSS/HIPAA/SOC 2) and less manual Elasticsearch plumbing.

tools.name: Security Onion
tools.desc: Turnkey NSM distribution bundling Suricata (detection + full packet capture), Zeek metadata, Elastic/Kibana dashboards, osquery host visibility, and alert/case management into a single guided install.
tools.when: Fastest way to stand up a whole detection-and-response platform on one box when you don't want to assemble SIEM, IDS, and ingestion yourself.
tools.install: Download the ISO from https://securityonion.com, install, then run: sudo so-setup-network (guided wizard)

tools.name: Graylog
tools.desc: Open-source log management and SIEM on Elasticsearch/OpenSearch storage, with flexible extraction pipelines (streams + pipeline rules) for parsing, enrichment, GEOIP, and threat-intel tagging.
tools.when: Log centralization when you want clean server-side pipelines to poll, enrich, and route messages — without running a fleet of endpoint agents or Wazuh-style XDR.
tools.install: curl -L -o graylog-repo.deb https://packages.graylog2.org/repo/packages/graylog-7.1-repository_latest.deb && sudo dpkg -i graylog-repo.deb && sudo apt-get install graylog-server

tools.name: Velociraptor
tools.desc: Open-source DFIR + endpoint-monitoring framework (Rapid7): fleet-wide hunts over VQL, live evidence collection across thousands of hosts, and a monitoring engine running Sigma detections against ETW/eBPF events in real time.
tools.when: Endpoint hunt and incident response at scale — triage every host, collect volatile evidence, then keep them watched with live detections; often the 'endpoint SIEM' half of a free SOC.

tools.name: Splunk Free
tools.desc: Free perpetual tier of the commercial SIEM incumbent: SPL search over indexed events and mature dashboards/alerts, capped at 500 MB/day ingest; a full license scales past the cap.
tools.when: When you want enterprise SIEM UX and Splunk's integration ecosystem at zero cost for a lab or small estate, or as the benchmark when evaluating an all-open stack.

tools.name: Velociraptor
tools.desc: Open-source endpoint visibility and collection platform: deploy lightweight agents, run prebuilt forensic artifacts and fleet-wide VQL hunts, push live Sigma/EQL detections, and pull processes, disk, and registry data to a central server.
tools.when: Hunt across every host you own in one place: stand up the server, enroll agents, and answer 'what happened here' with fleet-wide queries and persistent monitoring.

tools.name: osquery
tools.desc: SQL-powered agent exposing OS state — processes, sockets, files, users, listeners — as queryable tables; fire fleet-wide queries instantly and schedule packs, managed via Fleet (FleetDM).
tools.when: Lightweight cross-platform telemetry when you want to 'SELECT' answers from every host and ship results to SIEM; the armchair-friendly complement to Velociraptor.

tools.name: Sysmon
tools.desc: Windows Sysinternals driver that logs high-fidelity process creation, network connections, and file writes beyond default auditing; pair with the SwiftOnSecurity or Modular config for a solid hunting baseline.
tools.when: On every Windows host where you need attacker-action visibility and can ship its event log to your SIEM — no heavy agent required.

tools.name: LimaCharlie
tools.desc: Cloud-native SecOps platform: an EDR sensor streams verbose endpoint telemetry over TLS in real time, and a YAML-based Detection & Response engine runs the full open Sigma ruleset with automated response actions.
tools.when: When you want EDR plus detection-as-code in the cloud without running a SIEM or agent server yourself; the free Community org covers small estates and labs.
tools.install: preinstalled (cloud SaaS) — create a free Community org at limacharlie.io, run the per-OS sensor installer, and enable the Sigma ruleset

tools.name: RITA
tools.desc: Active Countermeasures' open-source network-traffic analysis framework that ingests Zeek logs and scores beaconing, long connections, DNS tunneling, and threat-intel hits for hunting C2.
tools.when: Turn passive Zeek metadata into C2 hunting: run it against captured or rolling Zeek logs to surface beacons and suspicious external connections a normal SIEM query would miss.
tools.install: Download the installer from https://github.com/activecm/rita/releases, then: tar -xf rita-<version>-installer.tar.gz && sudo ./rita-*/install_rita.sh

tools.name: Zeek
tools.desc: Passive network-analysis framework (formerly Bro) feeding rich protocol metadata, file hashes, and events to hunting and SIEM pipelines via 70+ log types — the data source RITA and BZAR consume.
tools.when: The metadata layer for hunt stacks: deploy the sensor, let its conn/dns/http logs flow into Elastic or RITA, and never push raw packets for every question.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install zeek (zeek.org apt repo) or docker pull zeek/zeek

tools.name: Suricata
tools.desc: OISF's multi-threaded open-source IDS/IPS engine inspecting traffic with Snort-compatible rules at multi-Gbps speeds and emitting structured EVE JSON alerts (plus PCAP) straight into your SIEM.
tools.when: High-throughput signature detection at your network edge or segmentation points; the default self-managed NIDS with an IPS fallback.
tools.install: sudo add-apt-repository ppa:oisf/suricata-stable && sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install suricata && sudo suricata-update

tools.name: Snort 3
tools.desc: Cisco's next-generation open-source NIDS/IPS: multi-threaded, Lua-based policy language, faster pattern matching than 2.x, tuned with Talos rules.
tools.when: When you prefer Cisco's Talos rule ecosystem, are migrating an existing Snort 2 deployment, or want SnortML-driven engine tuning.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install snort3 (Ubuntu 22.04+; otherwise build from the source tarball on snort.org)

tools.name: Zeek
tools.desc: Passive network-analysis framework (formerly Bro) that logs rich protocol metadata, file hashes, and events across 70+ log types for later forensics instead of blocking in real time.
tools.when: Deep protocol visibility feeding a SIEM or full-packet archive — run it beside Suricata/Snort because Zeek answers 'what happened' while the IDS engine answers 'alert'.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install zeek (zeek.org apt repo) or docker pull zeek/zeek

tools.name: tshark
tools.desc: Wireshark's terminal sibling: captures, decrypts, and prints live or offline traffic with the full dissector set and CSV/JSON/raw output for scripted analysis.
tools.when: Get Wireshark-grade dissection piped into grep, jq, or detection pipelines without a GUI — the workhorse for carving answers out of PCAP on servers and sensors.

tools.name: tcpdump
tools.desc: Command-line packet capture using Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) expressions; the standard for headless logging and scripted sniffing on any host.
tools.when: Rolling capture on a sensor, router, or lab box where no GUI exists, or when you need a quick BPF-filtered sniff to confirm what is on the wire.

tools.name: Auditd
tools.desc: Linux Audit framework userspace (auditd, auditctl, ausearch) recording privileged actions, file access, and security-relevant events to an immutable log across reboots.
tools.when: Build the audit trail that CIS/STIG rules require on Linux hosts and answer 'who accessed what, when' during a response with ausearch.

tools.name: Logstash
tools.desc: Data-shaping pipeline (the 'L' in ELK) that pulls logs and metrics, parses, enriches, filters, and routes them to Elasticsearch or any other output.
tools.when: The parsing/enrichment middle layer when an agent's native handling is not enough for messy or appliance-shaped log sources heading into Elastic.

tools.name: Sigma
tools.desc: The generic, SIEM-agnostic detection format: YAML rules describing log semantics; sigma-cli compiles them to Splunk, Elastic, Loki, MS Sentinel, and dozens of query languages from the SigmaHQ public rule set.
tools.when: Author one detection and ship it everywhere: port a SigmaHQ rule, run sigma convert --target <siem>, and validate the query against live logs before tuning.
tools.install: pipx install sigma-cli && git clone https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma

tools.name: CAR
tools.desc: MITRE's Cyber Analytics Repository: a knowledge base of validated analytics that pair each ATT&CK technique with a hypothesis, pseudocode, and concrete implementations (Splunk, EQL, Zeek).
tools.when: Harvest battle-tested analytic ideas to port into Sigma or your SIEM — read the operating theory and data model before writing new rules from scratch.

tools.name: Atomic Red Team
tools.desc: Red Canary's adversary-simulation library mapping hundreds of ATT&CK techniques to executable test definitions; each atomic documents the exact procedure and the telemetry a detection should fire on.
tools.when: Prove a Sigma/SIEM rule actually fires by running the matching atomic test and watching your alert pipeline — the purple-team workflow lives in the purpleteam domain.

tools.name: YARA
tools.desc: Binary pattern-matching rule engine for malware families and byte-level IOCs; complements SIEM rules when the evidence is a dropped file, not a log (fuller coverage in the malware domain).
tools.when: Match captured samples or suspicious files against signature rules, or encode a family signature your log-query team can't express in Sigma.

tools.name: Shuffle
tools.desc: Open-source SOAR platform: drag-and-drop workflow builder wiring apps, triggers, and actions to automate alert triage, enrichment calls, and response playbooks against your SIEM and intel tools.
tools.when: Automate repeatable analyst actions (enrich an IOC, quarantine a host, open a ticket) with a free self-hosted SOAR instead of hand-scripted glue.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/shuffle/shuffle && cd shuffle && docker compose up -d

tools.name: n8n
tools.desc: Fair-code workflow automation platform with 400+ integrations and a visual editor; a flexible general engine for chaining webhooks, email, HTTP APIs, and internal tools.
tools.when: Lighter-weight automation when Shuffle feels security-specific but you still want playbooks, schedules, and HTTP-triggered workflows in one self-hosted box.

tools.name: TheHive
tools.desc: Open-source security incident-response platform (TheHive 5) for collecting, sharing, and analyzing alerts as collaborative cases with tasks, observables, and full audit history.
tools.when: Track active incidents and alerts with structured cases, then close the loop by pushing findings back into detection tuning.

tools.name: Cortex
tools.desc: Open-source analyzer engine (TheHive companion): responders and analyzers run one-shot enrichments — DNS, hash lookups, intel feeds, quarantines — from TheHive, MISP, or its REST API.
tools.when: Standardized IOC enrichment as analyzers you can call from TheHive cases, MISP, or your SOAR playbooks without wiring each vendor API yourself.

tools.name: CISA Incident Response Playbooks
tools.desc: CISA's Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks: role-by-role, phase-by-phase response guidance with ready-to-copy templates for incident handling.
tools.when: Start with these when writing your own playbooks — lift the phases, roles, and communications plan, then adapt the details to your estate.

tools.name: NIST SP 800-61r3
tools.desc: NIST Special Publication 800-61 revision 3: incident-response recommendations and considerations for cybersecurity risk management — organizing IR, handling evidence, and coordination guidance.
tools.when: A defensible framework for how response teams should be structured and measured, whether you are building a small SOC or a whole CSIRT.

tools.name: Canarytokens
tools.desc: Thinkst's free hosted (or self-hosted Docker) tripwire factory generating DNS, URL, document (PDF/Word), AWS-key, QR-code, and Slack tokens that alert instantly when touched.
tools.when: When a full honeypot is overkill: sprinkle fake DNS names, URLs, or documents across AD, share drives, and public infra for cheap, near-instant detection of unauthorized access.
tools.install: preinstalled (canarytokens.org) — self-host: git clone https://github.com/thinkst/canarytokens-docker && cd canarytokens-docker && docker compose up

tools.name: OpenCanary
tools.desc: Thinkst's open-source multi-protocol honeypot daemon (SSH, telnet, HTTP, FTP, SNMP, SMB, RDP, MySQL) firing syslog, email, Slack, and webhook alerts on any probe; the OSS sibling of commercial Thinkst Canary.
tools.when: Drop a near-zero-footprint daemon on a jump host, file server, or DMZ for alerting on unexpected interaction — richer coverage lives in the honeypots domain.

tools.name: rspamd
tools.desc: Fast open-source mail filter scoring incoming message content with Bayesian/spamassassin rules, and signing outbound mail with DKIM plus DMARC/SRS support via its own Milter interface.
tools.when: Harden your own postfix/exim MTA: filter inbound spam and authenticate outbound with DKIM signing and SPF/DMARC alignment in one service.
tools.install: sudo add-apt-repository ppa:rspamd/rspamd && sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install rspamd

tools.name: checkdmarc
tools.desc: Python module/CLI validating SPF and DMARC DNS records end-to-end, including SPF lookup counts and void lookups, DMARC effectiveness warnings, MTA-STS, DANE/TLSA, and BIMI checks.
tools.when: Audit your own domain's email authentication posture before or after publishing records — run it defensively to catch a policy an attacker or vendor broke.

tools.name: swaks
tools.desc: Swiss Army Knife for SMTP: crafts arbitrary test messages with full control over sender, headers, attachments, and TLS to verify mail relays and backend behavior on hosts you administer.
tools.when: Verify an MTA or relay does what it should — test who can relay, check headers and SPF/DKIM passing, or reproduce a delivery issue from your own mail server.

tools.name: CrowdSec
tools.desc: Open-source crowd-sourced IPS (Suricata-aware): watches logs and events locally, bans offending IPs via bouncers at the firewall/nginx/cloud level, and shares signals through the community blocklist.
tools.when: Active response at the edge — replace dumb fail2ban-style blocking with attack-originated, shareable banishment backed by community signals.
tools.install: curl -s https://install.crowdsec.net | sudo sh && sudo cscli collections install crowdsecurity/linux && sudo systemctl start crowdsec

tools.name: Fail2ban
tools.desc: Classic log-scrape intrusion-prevention daemon that watches services (ssh, nginx, postfix) and bans repeat offenders through the host firewall or iptables backends.
tools.when: Simple, well-understood scoring-based banning on a single host — perfect when CrowdSec's community-signal model is more than you need.

tools.name: ModSecurity
tools.desc: The OWASP open-source WAF engine (an OWASP Production project) inspecting HTTP and enforcing SecRule policies on Apache/nginx; load the OWASP CRS on top for real attack coverage.
tools.when: Inline HTTP-layer defense when you want the battle-tested rule ecosystem and can commit to tuning false positives against your own apps.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install libapache2-mod-security2 (Apache; for nginx compile the module with --with-compat --add-dynamic-module=../ModSecurity-nginx)

tools.name: Coraza
tools.desc: OWASP WAF written in Go with near-full ModSecurity compatibility — runs CRS v4 without the legacy C engine as a library or middleware for Caddy, Traefik, APISIX, and API gateways.
tools.when: Cloud-native stacks (Go services, containers, Caddy/Traefik/APISIX) where ModSecurity's build model is awkward but you still want CRS protection.
tools.install: xcaddy build --with github.com/corazawaf/coraza-caddy/v2 (then add the coraza_waf block to the Caddyfile)

tools.name: OWASP CRS
tools.desc: The OWASP flagship Core Rule Set — a community-maintained rule layer detecting SQLi, XSS, scanners, and OWASP Top 10 attacks that runs on both ModSecurity and Coraza engines; a ruleset, not a standalone tool.
tools.when: The rule layer to load onto any WAF engine so a bare install actually detects web attacks; tune via the anomaly-scoring exclusions to cut false positives.
tools.install: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/coreruleset/coreruleset.git (then Include the CRS config in your WAF engine)

tools.name: Cloudflare WAF
tools.desc: Commercial managed edge WAF (SaaS) filtering traffic on Cloudflare's CDN with managed rulesets (including OWASP CRS coverage) plus bot and rate controls — no servers to run.
tools.when: When your apps already sit behind Cloudflare and you want managed rules, DDoS/bot defense, and zero self-hosting in one panel.
tools.install: preinstalled (SaaS) — enable in the dash.cloudflare.com Security panel, pick a managed ruleset, and tune via custom rules
